prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

Through stream-of-consciousness and surreal imagery, the passage explores workplace exploitation, gendered vulnerability, family responsibility, and fear of death. Its collapsing boundaries between bosses, paperwork, caregiving, and mortality reveal the inadequacy of money and documents to protect anyone, while small acts like dyeing one’s hair become desperate assertions of life.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: The

outputs.L1:
The boss is sitting at the desk. The boss doesn’t look at her. The boss is waiting for the black telephone to ring; she, too, waits for a ring from the boss. He is waiting for the files from her—her blue dress like a reused file folder wrapped around her body, her hands tight around the files. The filing cabinet might eat her, might take her hand off. The boss might eat her. The boss wants her, but the boss wants money more—just a little bit more. The boss always seems to want the money a bit more.

The boss doesn’t hear that there are taxis outside, waiting for all the women down on the street. Across the street, a boss prepares for bed. Another boss, above him in Apartment X, rotates a Q-tip in his ear before sex, despite the instructions on the box.

We took my father out of the paper—the living will. The letters, with their little capes, will leave the paper. Who will take care of my children later? Who will take care of my father? The will will take care of no one. A piece of paper cannot take care of anyone. I cannot take care of everyone.

On some nights, I wake in a panic and can’t tell whether I am dead or alive. This year, I dye my hair so I won’t have to die.
outputs.L2:
Behind the desk, the boss sits without glancing at her, expecting the black phone to sound. She, too, waits for the boss to call. He expects her to deliver the files. Her blue dress wraps her body like a folder used before, while she grips the documents with both hands. The filing cabinet could swallow her or sever her hand; the boss could devour her as well. He desires her, but he desires money slightly more. Somehow, money always matters just a little more to him.

He does not notice the taxis outside, lined up for all the women on the street below. Across the way, one boss gets ready for sleep. In apartment X, directly above him, another boss twists a cotton swab inside his ear before having sex, ignoring the warning printed on the package.

We removed my father from the document—the living will. The letters, wearing their tiny cloaks, will lift away from the page. Who will look after my children in the future? Who will care for my father? A will cares for nobody. No sheet of paper is capable of caring for anyone, and I am unable to care for everybody. Some nights, I jolt awake terrified, uncertain whether I am alive or dead. This year, I color my hair so that dying will not be necessary.
outputs.L3:
The boss ignores the woman as he waits impatiently for the telephone to ring and for her to deliver the files. His attention is fixed on business, reducing her presence to another part of the office routine. Meanwhile, she appears tense and vulnerable. The filing cabinet itself seems threatening, but her deeper fear comes from the boss and the predatory authority he exercises over her.

Although the boss desires the woman, that desire is secondary to his hunger for money. His financial appetite appears even stronger—and perhaps impossible to satisfy. The scene then expands beyond these two figures, revealing other women and other bosses performing similar routines. Across the workplace, labor, sexual desire, exploitation, and emotional indifference become part of the same repetitive system.

From this impersonal world, the speaker turns toward mortality and family. They reflect on a father’s living will and on the limits of legal documents: such papers can record instructions and distribute responsibility, but they cannot love, comfort, or care for the people left behind. This awareness leads to a more personal admission of the speaker’s fear of death. Dyeing their hair becomes a small act of resistance—a way of concealing age, asserting control over the body, and temporarily denying the approach of mortality.
outputs.L4:
The passage uses stream-of-consciousness narration and surreal imagery to portray a world in which work, family obligations, and fear of death become inseparably entangled. Thoughts move rapidly between bosses, paperwork, money, caregiving, and mortality, reproducing the pressure felt by someone who is never allowed to attend to a single crisis at a time. The breakdown of logical boundaries is not merely stylistic; it reflects a life destabilized by exploitation and anxiety.

Workplace authority appears as both economic power and personal threat. The bosses control wages, time, and access to security, yet they offer no meaningful protection. This vulnerability is also gendered: the speaker must navigate expectations surrounding appearance, obedience, care, and emotional endurance while remaining exposed to judgment and coercion. Bureaucratic objects such as forms, contracts, and other documents promise order, but their authority proves hollow. They can record a person’s labor or define an obligation, yet they cannot guarantee dignity, safety, or survival.

Family responsibility deepens this sense of entrapment. Caregiving is shaped by affection, but also by guilt, exhaustion, and financial pressure. Money becomes necessary for sustaining life while remaining fundamentally inadequate to the task. It can pay bills or temporarily relieve hardship, but it cannot prevent illness, repair every damaged relationship, or keep death away. As the passage shifts between domestic and professional spaces, it shows how exploitation follows the speaker home and how private grief intrudes into the workplace.

Against this overwhelming system, small acts of self-fashioning acquire unusual importance. Dyeing one’s hair may seem trivial, but here it becomes a desperate assertion of vitality and control. When institutions reduce people to workers, dependents, signatures, or files, changing one’s appearance offers a way to insist on the living body and the individual will. The act cannot defeat exploitation or mortality, but it briefly declares that life is still present and that the self has not been entirely absorbed by duty and fear.

Ultimately, the passage presents modern existence as a precarious struggle against forces that cannot be mastered through wages, paperwork, or obedience. Its surreal movement reveals the emotional truth beneath ordinary routines: employment can become coercive, care can become burdensome, and bureaucracy can disguise rather than resolve human vulnerability. Yet the persistence of small, personal acts suggests a fragile resistance—a refusal to surrender completely, even in the face of death.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about office power, gender, money, legal documents, caregiving, and fear of death. Use breathless run-on sentences, repetition, and almost no punctuation.
counterfactuals.output:
at nine the elevator swallowed us by title and salary and spat us out by gender and shoes and who had learned to laugh at the right volume and who carried milk in a glass jar beside the stapler because someone at home was small and feverish and waiting and waiting and the director sat beneath a ficus made of green banknotes saying sign here sign here sign here while the contract grew teeth around the margins and the nondisclosure agreement folded itself into a white hospital sheet

we worked for money we worked for mercy we worked because money had keys to the pharmacy and mercy did not and every spreadsheet opened like a chapel where the cells were tiny graves and the numbers knelt in rows and the bonus floated above us like an angel with a man’s voice and a woman’s calendar and no face at all

in the conference room power poured coffee for itself and called this kindness while she took notes while he took credit while they changed the language from command to collaboration and back again and the legal department sent a document longer than winter defining mother defining worker defining reasonable defining loss and no one could find the clause for holding a frightened hand at three in the morning

sign here sign here the pen whispered though the pen was a thermometer though the pen was a needle though the pen was the thin black oar with which we rowed across the dark toward payday toward daycare toward the blinking machines beside the bed

and all day death waited politely in reception wearing a visitor badge and reading last quarter’s report and all day we pretended not to know its name though it knew our salaries and our passwords and the soft exact weight of every person we could not afford to lose

so we answered emails we answered alarms we answered mother father sir ma’am team lead counsel dependent we answered until our mouths became office doors opening opening and behind each door another signature another child calling another old body turning toward the wall another invoice another promise that the company was a family

the company was a family the company was a family the company was a family

and the family had no heart only policies

and still we brought soup

and still we signed

and still the elevator rose with its silver throat full of us breathing too quickly counting our money counting our pills counting the days we had left though no one had given us that number no one no one no one
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental stream-of-consciousness monologue that begins with a boss and secretary waiting in an office, then drifts into city apartments, a father’s living will, anxiety about children, and dyeing one’s hair to resist mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
The boss waits behind the desk and the secretary waits in front of it, though either could be said to be waiting for the other, or for the telephone, or for the thin gray afternoon to make up its mind. Between them sits a glass paperweight with a trapped blue flower. The boss looks at the clock. The secretary looks at the boss looking at the clock. Somewhere in the building, water travels through pipes with the confidence of something that has been given instructions.

No one speaks.

Across the street, apartments rise window over window, small illuminated proofs of other lives: a woman shaking crumbs from a cloth, a man bending to tie a shoe, a child holding a red balloon indoors. How dangerous, a balloon indoors. How easily it might touch the ceiling and remain there, unreachable, like a thought one had meant to finish. Above them, on the ninth floor, someone paints a wall yellow. On the twelfth, someone has not unpacked for six years. Boxes marked BOOKS, WINTER, MOTHER. The city is full of people storing earlier versions of themselves in closets.

The secretary thinks perhaps the boss will say, You may go.

The boss thinks perhaps the secretary already has.

My father’s living will was in a green folder beside the toaster, which seemed the wrong place for it, though what is the right place for instructions concerning the end of a body? Not with the tax returns. Not under the socks. He had underlined *no extraordinary measures* twice, as if death were a clerk likely to misunderstand. No machines, no tubes, no heroic interventions. Heroic: the word bothered me. As though love, frightened and sleepless in a plastic chair, might become villainy merely by asking for another hour.

He signed his name firmly. The signature looked healthier than he did.

Outside, buses exhale at the curb. Elevators open and close on empty halls. In one apartment a baby coughs, and three rooms away a mother wakes before the sound is finished. This is the curse of children: they continue inside you after leaving your body. They cross streets in cities where you cannot see the traffic. They climb chairs, swallow coins, love strangers, board airplanes, mistake loneliness for destiny. You warn them about outlets, deep water, men who say trust me, women who say I’m fine, the hereditary weakness in the left knee. Still they run ahead.

What if the child’s fever rises?

What if the child has no fever and I invent one?

What if vigilance is only another name for fear wearing a uniform?

The boss clears his throat. The secretary straightens, and for a moment the whole office leans toward speech. But the boss only asks whether it is raining. The secretary says she doesn’t know. Neither turns toward the window.

Yesterday I found a white hair at my temple, bright as wire. Then another. By evening there were hundreds, an uprising I had somehow failed to notice. I bought dye called Eternal Chestnut, though chestnuts rot and eternity has never been brown. In the bathroom mirror I mixed the chemicals, squeezed the bottle, pulled on gloves thin as second thoughts. The smell was sharp, medicinal, almost festive.

I painted youth onto my head.

Not youth exactly—its alibi.

Dark streams ran down my forehead, and I thought of my father’s green folder, of blue veins under paper skin, of children asleep in high rooms while the city kept lifting and dropping its elevators. I thought: this is foolish. I thought: leave it on five more minutes. I thought mortality might be resisted in increments, at the roots, every four to six weeks.

The boss waits. The secretary waits. The blue flower remains perfectly preserved beneath glass, which is not the same as being alive, though from a distance, in the failing light, it is difficult to tell.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a fragmented feminist prose poem in which “the boss” is repeated obsessively, a blue dress resembles a file folder, filing cabinets become threatening, and paperwork fails to protect loved ones.
counterfactuals.output:
The boss says the blue dress is professional. The boss says smile. The boss says not like that.

The blue dress hangs from my shoulders like a file folder—creased, labeled, manila-blue, impossible blue—my body misfiled beneath it.

The boss opens a drawer.

The boss closes a drawer.

The boss has a key for every metal mouth.

In Cabinet A: my hours.  
In Cabinet B: my silence.  
In Cabinet C: the names of women who learned to become paper before paper could become them.

The boss says protocol. The boss says policy. The boss says sign here, here, and here. The boss says the form will protect us.

Us, the boss says, meaning the building.

I sign for my mother’s medicine. I sign for my sister’s leave. I sign the emergency contact card in ink so black it resembles a small locked door.

Still, the phone rings.

Still, the form returns stamped INCOMPLETE.

Still, my loved ones stand outside the paragraph where help was promised.

The filing cabinets grow after dark. Their drawers slide open by themselves, long silver tongues. They know our maiden names. They know which of us complained. They know the date, the time, the blouse, the witness who suddenly remembers nothing.

The boss says there is no record.

The boss says the record is confidential.

The boss says the record cannot be located.

The boss, the boss, the boss—three staples through the soft corner of a day.

I wear the blue dress because the handbook says blue is calm. Because anger must be dressed as weather. Because a woman in red is evidence, a woman in black is difficult, a woman in blue can be filed under compliant.

But the dress has tabs now.

GRIEF.  
WAGES.  
TOUCH.  
DO NOT DESTROY.

The boss reaches for the drawer.

I put my hand on it.

All around us, paper trembles—thin, official, useless as snow against a burning house.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write one dense paragraph of surreal literary fiction with no conventional sentence breaks. Include a black telephone, taxis waiting for women, a Q-tip used before sex, letters escaping from a living will, and a narrator unsure whether they are alive or dead.
counterfactuals.output: At midnight the black telephone began ringing inside the locked aquarium, each pulse releasing a small blue moon that rose through the ceiling where taxis waited for women in red gloves who never emerged from the hotel, and I stood before the mirror with a Q-tip poised like a tiny white torch, performing the obscure ritual she insisted upon before sex, though her bed had long since filled with rain and moths, while on the desk my living will shuddered awake and its letters escaped in black processions, crawling over my wrists, slipping beneath the door, rearranging themselves along the corridor into instructions I could not obey, because the voice in the telephone was mine but older, whispering that the drivers had been dead for years, that the women were only their destinations, that the aquarium contained the last clean air in the city, and as the receiver floated toward me through the glass I could not remember whether I had drowned beside the bed or merely dreamed my funeral, whether this breath belonged to a body or to the page describing it, whether I was alive and imagining death or dead and still unable to stop imagining myself
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an unsettling, punctuation-free poem about workplace objectification and family responsibility, moving associatively from money and files to a dying father, helplessness, nighttime panic, and the final line: “this year I dye my hair so I won’t have to die.”
counterfactuals.output:
they count my hours in small metal mouths  
and slide my name beneath the money  

the files open like pale knees  
every tab a place to be handled  
every signature another hand  
asking me to smile while it searches  

I keep photographs facedown in my drawer  
mother at the sink  
my brother holding the roof up with his eyes  
father becoming lighter inside the hospital bed  

his lungs fill with unfinished invoices  
his pulse clocks out early  
I bring him water  
I bring him forms  
I bring him the helpless animal of my body  

nothing I carry can pay for morning  

at night the office follows me home  
the copier breathes in the hallway  
the phone rings under my pillow  
someone is pricing my face  
someone is filing my skin  

I wake with my hands around nothing  
the dark wearing my fathers voice  
saying hurry  
saying stay  
saying there is no correct answer  

this year I dye my hair so I won’t have to die.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
